frontHtml: A patient has a drooping mouth on one side but wrinkles the forehead normally. Where is the lesion?
backHtml: Upper motor neuron (cortex or corticobulbar tract) on the opposite side. The forehead part of the facial nucleus has bilateral cortical input.

frontHtml: Which facial nerve branch, lost in a lesion at or above the geniculate ganglion, causes a dry eye?
backHtml: The greater petrosal nerve (parasympathetic supply to the lacrimal gland).

frontHtml: Facial palsy plus a same-side abducens palsy and opposite-side limb weakness: where is the lesion?
backHtml: The pons (facial fibres loop around the abducens nucleus; the corticospinal tract has not yet crossed).

frontHtml: First-line treatment of Bell palsy seen within 72 hours of onset?
backHtml: An oral corticosteroid (for example, a 10-day prednisolone course), plus eye protection. No antiviral alone, no routine imaging.

frontHtml: Facial palsy with vesicles in the ear canal and hearing loss: diagnosis and treatment?
backHtml: Ramsay Hunt syndrome (herpes zoster oticus): a corticosteroid plus an antiviral such as valacyclovir.

frontHtml: Which features of an acute facial palsy call for imaging?
backHtml: Gradual progression over weeks, recurrence on the same side, other cranial nerve or limb signs, or a parotid mass.

frontHtml: Three leading causes of bacterial meningitis in the first month of life?
backHtml: Group B streptococcus, E. coli (K1 capsule) and Listeria monocytogenes.

frontHtml: Which meningococcal component causes septic shock and DIC?
backHtml: Lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin), shed in outer-membrane blebs.

frontHtml: Which immune defect predisposes to recurrent Neisseria infections?
backHtml: Terminal complement (C5–C9) deficiency; also asplenia and the C5 inhibitor eculizumab.

frontHtml: CSF in bacterial versus viral meningitis: the most reliable single difference?
backHtml: Glucose: low in bacterial (CSF:serum ratio below about 0.4), normal in viral.

frontHtml: Which organism needs ampicillin cover in meningitis, and in which patients?
backHtml: Listeria: neonates, adults over 50, pregnancy and impaired cell-mediated immunity.

frontHtml: Which brain regions does HSV encephalitis target?
backHtml: Medial temporal lobes and orbitofrontal cortex (haemorrhagic necrosis).

frontHtml: How is acyclovir activated, and how does resistance arise?
backHtml: First phosphorylated by viral thymidine kinase; resistance comes from loss or alteration of that kinase (use foscarnet).

frontHtml: Pathological hallmark of prion disease?
backHtml: Spongiform vacuolation with neuronal loss and no inflammation; PrPSc is β-sheet rich and protease resistant.

frontHtml: Which HIV-related brain lesion does not enhance or cause mass effect?
backHtml: PML (JC virus infection of oligodendrocytes).

frontHtml: Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the basal ganglia in HIV with CD4 below 100: likely cause?
backHtml: Cerebral toxoplasmosis; a single periventricular lesion with EBV DNA in CSF suggests primary CNS lymphoma.

frontHtml: Argyll Robertson pupil?
backHtml: Small, irregular pupil that constricts to a near target but not to light; seen in neurosyphilis.

frontHtml: Where are MS plaques typically found on MRI?
backHtml: Periventricular (ovoid, perpendicular to the ventricles), juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord.

frontHtml: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia: lesion and findings?
backHtml: Medial longitudinal fasciculus: the eye on the lesion side cannot adduct, the abducting eye has nystagmus, convergence is spared.

frontHtml: Natalizumab: target and main risk?
backHtml: α4-integrin (blocks lymphocyte entry to the CNS); PML.

frontHtml: Which MS drugs cause first-dose bradycardia, and how do they lower lymphocyte counts?
backHtml: S1P receptor modulators (fingolimod, siponimod, ozanimod); they trap lymphocytes in lymph nodes.

frontHtml: Target antigen in NMOSD and the cell it injures?
backHtml: Aquaporin-4 on astrocyte foot processes.

frontHtml: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: classic patient and associated tumour?
backHtml: Young woman with psychiatric symptoms, seizures, dyskinesias and autonomic instability; ovarian teratoma.

frontHtml: When do the rostral and caudal neuropores close?
backHtml: Rostral about day 25; caudal about day 27–28.

frontHtml: Which neural tube defects raise AFP, and which does not?
backHtml: Open defects (anencephaly, open myelomeningocele) raise AFP; skin-covered spina bifida occulta does not.

frontHtml: Chiari I versus Chiari II?
backHtml: Chiari I: tonsillar descent, adolescents and adults, cough headache, syrinx. Chiari II: vermis and medulla herniate, myelomeningocele and hydrocephalus at birth.

frontHtml: Dandy-Walker malformation: three features?
backHtml: Hypoplastic vermis, cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle, enlarged posterior fossa.

frontHtml: Holoprosencephaly: signalling defect and two associations?
backHtml: Sonic hedgehog; trisomy 13 and prenatal alcohol (also maternal diabetes).

frontHtml: NF1 gene product and function?
backHtml: Neurofibromin (chromosome 17), a GTPase-activating protein that switches off Ras.

frontHtml: Hallmark tumour of NF2-related schwannomatosis?
backHtml: Bilateral vestibular schwannomas (also meningiomas and ependymomas).

frontHtml: Tuberous sclerosis: pathway and four non-CNS lesions?
backHtml: mTOR overactivity; cardiac rhabdomyoma, renal angiomyolipoma, facial angiofibromas, hypomelanotic macules (also LAM).

frontHtml: Sturge-Weber syndrome: genetic cause and skin sign?
backHtml: Somatic activating GNAQ mutation; port-wine stain in the V1 distribution.

frontHtml: Why does preterm periventricular leukomalacia cause spastic diplegia?
backHtml: The corticospinal fibres to the legs run closest to the lateral ventricles.

frontHtml: Six findings that call for CT before lumbar puncture in suspected meningitis?
backHtml: Immunocompromise, known CNS disease, seizure in the past week, papilledema, reduced consciousness, focal deficit.

frontHtml: If CT must come first, what happens before the scan?
backHtml: Blood cultures, then dexamethasone and empirical antibiotics; do not delay treatment for imaging.

frontHtml: Empirical meningitis therapy for a 30-year-old? For a 70-year-old?
backHtml: 30: vancomycin + ceftriaxone. 70: vancomycin + ceftriaxone + ampicillin.

frontHtml: Chemoprophylaxis options for close contacts of meningococcal disease?
backHtml: Single-dose oral ciprofloxacin, 2 days of rifampin, or single-dose IM ceftriaxone.

frontHtml: Should acyclovir wait for the HSV PCR result in suspected encephalitis?
backHtml: No. Start intravenous acyclovir on suspicion; repeat PCR if an early test is negative and suspicion stays high.

frontHtml: Cryptococcal meningitis: induction therapy and pressure control?
backHtml: Amphotericin B (liposomal) + flucytosine; repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures. Delay ART about 4–6 weeks.

frontHtml: When should a presumed toxoplasmosis lesion in HIV be biopsied?
backHtml: If it does not improve after about 2 weeks of pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin.

frontHtml: Treatment of neurosyphilis?
backHtml: Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days (desensitise if allergic).

frontHtml: Key test after a first episode of optic neuritis?
backHtml: MRI of the brain with gadolinium, to assess MS risk and dissemination in space.

frontHtml: MS patient with old symptoms returning plus fever and dysuria: next step?
backHtml: Urinalysis and culture; treat the infection (pseudo-relapse), not with steroids.

frontHtml: Treatment of a disabling MS relapse? If it fails?
backHtml: High-dose methylprednisolone for 3–5 days; then plasma exchange.

frontHtml: Which MS drugs can worsen NMOSD?
backHtml: Interferon-β, natalizumab and fingolimod.

frontHtml: Screening test before starting an anti-CD20 antibody?
backHtml: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody (risk of reactivation).

frontHtml: Folic acid dose with no prior NTD versus after an affected pregnancy?
backHtml: 0.4–0.8 mg daily versus 4 mg daily, from at least 1 month before conception.

frontHtml: Immediate care of a newborn with an open myelomeningocele?
backHtml: Sterile saline-moistened dressing, prone positioning, latex-free care, antibiotics if leaking, closure within about 48–72 hours.

frontHtml: Child with a VP shunt, vomiting and drowsiness: next step?
backHtml: Urgent brain imaging plus shunt series and neurosurgery; shunt failure until proven otherwise.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis?
backHtml: Vigabatrin (monitor for visual field loss).

frontHtml: Which antenatal drug reduces cerebral palsy risk in imminent birth before 32 weeks?
backHtml: Magnesium sulfate.

frontHtml: Treatment of focal spasticity limiting gait in cerebral palsy?
backHtml: Botulinum toxin injections with stretching, casting or orthoses.

frontHtml: Most common primary brain tumour in adults? Most common malignant one?
backHtml: Meningioma; glioblastoma (but metastases outnumber all primary tumours).

frontHtml: Where do most brain tumours arise in adults and in children?
backHtml: Adults: supratentorial. Children: posterior fossa (cerebellum, fourth ventricle, brainstem).

frontHtml: Which primary CNS tumours seed the spinal leptomeninges through CSF?
backHtml: Medulloblastoma, ependymoma and germinoma ("drop metastases").

frontHtml: Why do posterior fossa tumours present early with vomiting and headache on waking?
backHtml: They obstruct the fourth ventricle and cause obstructive hydrocephalus with raised intracranial pressure.

frontHtml: Meningioma: cell of origin and two histology clues?
backHtml: Arachnoid cap cells; whorls and psammoma bodies. EMA and progesterone receptor positive.

frontHtml: Schwannoma histology?
backHtml: Cellular Antoni A areas with palisaded nuclei (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas; S-100 positive.

frontHtml: Cyst with a mural nodule in the cerebellum: child versus adult?
backHtml: Child: pilocytic astrocytoma (Rosenthal fibres). Adult: hemangioblastoma (VHL; may cause polycythemia).

frontHtml: Gene and protein function in von Hippel–Lindau disease?
backHtml: VHL on chromosome 3p; the protein targets hypoxia-inducible factor for degradation.

frontHtml: Craniopharyngioma: origin and classic triad of findings in a child?
backHtml: Rathke pouch remnant. Bitemporal field loss, growth failure (hypopituitarism) and a calcified suprasellar cyst.

frontHtml: What is the pituitary stalk effect?
backHtml: Compression of the stalk cuts off hypothalamic dopamine, so prolactin rises modestly (usually below about 150 ng/mL) with a nonfunctioning adenoma.

frontHtml: Glioblastoma: two histologic hallmarks?
backHtml: Pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation.

frontHtml: Which molecular features define oligodendroglioma (WHO CNS5)?
backHtml: IDH mutation plus 1p/19q codeletion.

frontHtml: What does mutant IDH produce, and what does that product do?
backHtml: 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits α-ketoglutarate–dependent demethylases, causing hypermethylation and blocked differentiation.

frontHtml: Why does MGMT promoter methylation predict response to temozolomide?
backHtml: It silences MGMT, the enzyme that removes temozolomide's methyl adducts from guanine.

frontHtml: Medulloblastoma: site, histology and marker?
backHtml: Cerebellar vermis in children; small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes; synaptophysin positive.

frontHtml: Ependymoma: characteristic microscopic structure?
backHtml: Perivascular pseudorosettes (cells around vessels with a nucleus-free fibrillary zone).

frontHtml: Primary CNS lymphoma in advanced HIV: cell type and virus?
backHtml: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma driven by Epstein–Barr virus.

frontHtml: Most common sources of brain metastases?
backHtml: Lung (most common), breast, melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, colorectal.

frontHtml: Which brain metastases tend to bleed?
backHtml: Melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid carcinoma.

frontHtml: Anti-Yo antibody: tumour and syndrome?
backHtml: Ovarian or breast carcinoma; subacute cerebellar degeneration.

frontHtml: Anti-Hu antibody: tumour and syndromes?
backHtml: Small cell lung carcinoma; encephalomyelitis and sensory neuronopathy.

frontHtml: Why do anti-NMDA receptor syndromes respond to immunotherapy while anti-Hu syndromes rarely do?
backHtml: NMDA receptor is on the cell surface, so the antibody is pathogenic. Hu is intracellular; T cells cause irreversible neuron loss.

frontHtml: Best imaging test for a suspected brain tumour?
backHtml: MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium (CT first only in an emergency).

frontHtml: Should a patient with a brain tumour and no seizures receive antiseizure prophylaxis?
backHtml: No. Treat only after a seizure; prefer levetiracetam (non–enzyme-inducing).

frontHtml: Standard treatment of glioblastoma in a fit patient?
backHtml: Maximal safe resection, then focal radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide.

frontHtml: Suspected primary CNS lymphoma in a stable patient: what to avoid before biopsy?
backHtml: Corticosteroids; they can shrink the lymphoma and make the biopsy nondiagnostic.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of a macroprolactinoma that causes visual field loss?
backHtml: A dopamine agonist, cabergoline.

frontHtml: First step in pituitary apoplexy with hypotension?
backHtml: Stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone, then neurosurgical evaluation.

frontHtml: New enhancement within the radiation field 6 weeks after glioblastoma chemoradiation in a well patient?
backHtml: Suspect pseudoprogression: continue temozolomide and repeat MRI.

frontHtml: Child with morning vomiting, ataxia and papilledema: next step?
backHtml: MRI of the brain before any lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: How is medulloblastoma staged?
backHtml: MRI of the whole spine and CSF cytology, plus postoperative brain MRI.

frontHtml: Yearly surveillance in a young child with NF1?
backHtml: Ophthalmologic examination (optic pathway glioma) and blood pressure at every visit.

frontHtml: Treatment of a cerebellar pilocytic astrocytoma?
backHtml: Complete surgical resection, usually curative.

frontHtml: Cancer patient with back pain and new leg weakness: first two actions?
backHtml: Dexamethasone now and emergency MRI of the whole spine.

frontHtml: Cord compression from myeloma or lymphoma in a stable spine: definitive treatment?
backHtml: Radiotherapy (radiosensitive tumours); surgery for instability or radioresistant tumours.

frontHtml: Single accessible symptomatic brain metastasis in a fit patient?
backHtml: Resection followed by stereotactic radiosurgery to the cavity.

frontHtml: A few small brain metastases in a fit patient?
backHtml: Stereotactic radiosurgery (preserves cognition better than whole-brain radiotherapy).

frontHtml: How is leptomeningeal metastasis diagnosed?
backHtml: Gadolinium MRI of the brain and whole spine, then CSF cytology (repeat if negative).

frontHtml: Anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman: what tumour search?
backHtml: Pelvic MRI or transvaginal ultrasonography for an ovarian teratoma.

frontHtml: Leg weakness worse than arm, urinary incontinence and abulia: which artery?
backHtml: The anterior cerebral artery (medial frontal and parietal cortex, leg area of the motor and sensory strips).

frontHtml: Which way do the eyes deviate after a large hemispheric infarct?
backHtml: Toward the lesion (away from the weak side), because the frontal eye field that drives gaze to the opposite side is lost.

frontHtml: Why is central vision often spared in a posterior cerebral artery infarct?
backHtml: The occipital pole has dual supply, with collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery.

frontHtml: Proximal arm and thigh weakness after profound hypotension: where is the injury?
backHtml: Bilateral watershed (border-zone) infarcts between the anterior and middle cerebral territories.

frontHtml: Left-sided weakness with neglect of left space and denial of the deficit: which territory?
backHtml: The right (nondominant) middle cerebral artery.

frontHtml: In the lateral medullary syndrome, on which sides is pain and temperature lost?
backHtml: Same-side face (spinal trigeminal tract) and opposite-side body (crossed spinothalamic tract).

frontHtml: Which nucleus, damaged in a lateral medullary infarct, causes hoarseness and dysphagia?
backHtml: The nucleus ambiguus (motor to pharynx and larynx via IX and X).

frontHtml: In a medial medullary infarct, which way does the tongue deviate?
backHtml: Toward the side of the lesion (the weak genioglossus is pushed over by the normal side).

frontHtml: What preserved movements identify a locked-in patient?
backHtml: Vertical eye movements and blinking; the midbrain gaze centres are spared in a ventral pontine infarct.

frontHtml: Name the most common lacunar syndrome and its usual site.
backHtml: Pure motor hemiparesis of face, arm and leg: posterior limb of the internal capsule (or basis pontis).

frontHtml: Pure sensory stroke of the face, arm and leg: where is the lacune?
backHtml: The ventral posterolateral (and posteromedial) thalamus.

frontHtml: When do red neurons appear after an ischemic stroke?
backHtml: About 12–24 hours after the insult.

frontHtml: What type of necrosis does an infarct of the brain undergo?
backHtml: Liquefactive necrosis, leaving a glial-lined cyst.

frontHtml: Lobar hemorrhages in an older normotensive person: most likely cause?
backHtml: Cerebral amyloid angiopathy (beta-amyloid in cortical and leptomeningeal vessel walls).

frontHtml: Most common site of hypertensive intracerebral hemorrhage?
backHtml: The putamen (lenticulostriate arteries); then thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

frontHtml: Which inherited kidney disease is linked to saccular cerebral aneurysms?
backHtml: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease.

frontHtml: When does vasospasm after subarachnoid hemorrhage usually occur?
backHtml: About days 3–14 after the bleed.

frontHtml: What two kinds of lesion can cause coma?
backHtml: Damage to the upper brainstem tegmentum or thalamus (reticular activating system), or diffuse dysfunction of both hemispheres.

frontHtml: Eyes open with sleep–wake cycles but no awareness on repeated testing: what state?
backHtml: Unresponsive wakefulness (vegetative state).

frontHtml: Which neurons are most vulnerable to global hypoxic-ischemic injury?
backHtml: Hippocampal CA1 pyramidal cells, cerebellar Purkinje cells, and neocortical layers 3, 5 and 6.

frontHtml: Coma with pinpoint pupils and quadriplegia: where is the lesion?
backHtml: The pons (for example, a pontine hemorrhage).

frontHtml: Cold water in one ear of a comatose patient: what response shows an intact brainstem?
backHtml: Slow tonic deviation of both eyes toward the cold ear, without a fast corrective phase.

frontHtml: Biconvex hematoma that does not cross sutures: which space and vessel?
backHtml: Epidural; usually the middle meningeal artery after a temporal bone fracture.

frontHtml: Crescent-shaped hematoma that crosses sutures: which space and vessels?
backHtml: Subdural; torn bridging veins.

frontHtml: Deep coma after a high-speed rotational injury with a nearly normal CT: likely diagnosis?
backHtml: Diffuse axonal injury.

frontHtml: Name four signs of a basilar skull fracture.
backHtml: Mastoid bruising, periorbital bruising, blood behind the tympanic membrane, CSF leak from the nose or ear.

frontHtml: Formula for cerebral perfusion pressure?
backHtml: CPP = mean arterial pressure − intracranial pressure.

frontHtml: What three signs make up the Cushing reflex?
backHtml: Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing: a late sign of brainstem compression.

frontHtml: Uncal herniation: first cranial nerve sign and why?
backHtml: A fixed dilated pupil on the same side: compression of the oculomotor nerve, whose pupillary fibres lie superficially.

frontHtml: Which artery is compressed in subfalcine herniation, and what deficit results?
backHtml: The anterior cerebral artery: weakness of the opposite leg.

frontHtml: All four ventricles enlarged after meningitis: what type of hydrocephalus?
backHtml: Communicating hydrocephalus from scarred arachnoid granulations.

frontHtml: Triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus?
backHtml: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence and cognitive slowing.

frontHtml: Time window for IV thrombolysis in acute ischemic stroke?
backHtml: Within 4.5 hours of last known well.

frontHtml: Blood pressure limits around IV thrombolysis?
backHtml: Below 185/110 mm Hg before treatment and below 180/105 mm Hg for 24 hours after.

frontHtml: Which strokes benefit from endovascular thrombectomy?
backHtml: Large-vessel occlusion (internal carotid or proximal middle cerebral; also basilar), within 6 hours, and selected patients up to 24 hours.

frontHtml: Blood pressure threshold for treatment in acute ischemic stroke without thrombolysis?
backHtml: Treat only above about 220/120 mm Hg (permissive hypertension).

frontHtml: When is antiplatelet therapy started after IV thrombolysis?
backHtml: After 24 hours, once repeat imaging excludes hemorrhage.

frontHtml: Antithrombotic therapy for minor noncardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA?
backHtml: Aspirin plus clopidogrel started within 24 hours for about 21 days, then a single antiplatelet drug.

frontHtml: Stroke with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: preferred long-term therapy?
backHtml: A direct oral anticoagulant (for example, apixaban).

frontHtml: Indication for carotid endarterectomy after a TIA?
backHtml: Symptomatic stenosis of 70–99% (consider 50–69%), ideally within 2 weeks.

frontHtml: LDL cholesterol target after ischemic stroke of atherosclerotic origin?
backHtml: Below 70 mg/dL, with a high-intensity statin (add ezetimibe if needed).

frontHtml: How is warfarin reversed in intracerebral hemorrhage?
backHtml: Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K.

frontHtml: Specific reversal agent for dabigatran?
backHtml: Idarucizumab.

frontHtml: Thunderclap headache with a normal CT 10 hours later: next step?
backHtml: Lumbar puncture for xanthochromia and red cells that do not clear.

frontHtml: Which drug improves outcome after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage?
backHtml: Oral nimodipine for 21 days.

frontHtml: Treatment of cerebral venous thrombosis with a hemorrhagic venous infarct?
backHtml: Anticoagulation with heparin despite the hemorrhage.

frontHtml: Neck pain, partial Horner syndrome and a TIA after neck manipulation: diagnosis and treatment?
backHtml: Internal carotid dissection; antithrombotic therapy (antiplatelet or anticoagulant).

frontHtml: First bedside test in any comatose patient?
backHtml: A fingerstick glucose.

frontHtml: When can neurological prognosis be assessed after cardiac arrest?
backHtml: No sooner than about 72 hours, using several tests together.

frontHtml: Minimum core temperature before evaluating for death by neurologic criteria?
backHtml: At least 36 °C.

frontHtml: Apnea test thresholds for death by neurologic criteria?
backHtml: No breathing with PaCO2 at least 60 mm Hg and at least 20 mm Hg above baseline.

frontHtml: Are spinal reflexes compatible with brain death?
backHtml: Yes: for example, triple flexion of the legs can persist.

frontHtml: Which patients with a minor head injury need CT regardless of examination?
backHtml: Those taking anticoagulants or with a bleeding disorder (and others meeting decision-rule criteria).

frontHtml: Can an athlete return to play the same day after a concussion?
backHtml: No; remove from play and follow a graded, stepwise return once symptom-free.

frontHtml: Treatment of a symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma with mass effect?
backHtml: Burr-hole drainage.

frontHtml: Are glucocorticoids used in traumatic brain injury?
backHtml: No; they increase mortality.

frontHtml: Polyuria with dilute urine and hypernatremia after head injury: diagnosis and treatment?
backHtml: Central diabetes insipidus; desmopressin.

frontHtml: Step after first-tier measures for raised ICP in traumatic brain injury?
backHtml: CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol).

frontHtml: Role of hyperventilation in raised ICP?
backHtml: A brief bridge for impending herniation only (PaCO2 about 30–35 mm Hg).

frontHtml: Suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension: which test comes first?
backHtml: MRI of the brain with MR venography, then lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of idiopathic intracranial hypertension?
backHtml: Weight loss plus acetazolamide, with visual field monitoring.

frontHtml: Suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus: next step after imaging?
backHtml: A high-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) to predict shunt response.

frontHtml: Which spinal tract crosses within 1–2 segments of entry, and where?
backHtml: The spinothalamic tract: second-order axons cross in the anterior white commissure.

frontHtml: Right cord hemisection: which side loses pain and temperature, and which side is weak?
backHtml: Pain and temperature lost on the left (from 1–2 segments below); weakness and lost vibration/position sense on the right.

frontHtml: Which modality is preserved in anterior spinal artery infarction?
backHtml: Vibration and joint position sense (dorsal columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries).

frontHtml: Bilateral cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved touch: lesion and usual association?
backHtml: Syrinx damaging the anterior white commissure; often a Chiari I malformation.

frontHtml: Which tracts does subacute combined degeneration damage?
backHtml: Dorsal columns and lateral corticospinal tracts (plus peripheral nerves). Causes: B<sub>12</sub> or copper deficiency, nitrous oxide.

frontHtml: At what vertebral level does the adult spinal cord end?
backHtml: About L1–L2 (conus medullaris); lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.

frontHtml: A posterolateral L4–L5 disc herniation compresses which root?
backHtml: L5 (the root exiting one level lower).

frontHtml: Conus medullaris vs cauda equina: which has early symmetric saddle loss and early sphincter failure?
backHtml: Conus medullaris; cauda equina is gradual, asymmetric, painful and purely lower motor neuron.

frontHtml: Neurogenic shock: heart rate and skin?
backHtml: Bradycardia with warm, dry skin (lost sympathetic tone, unopposed vagus).

frontHtml: Above which cord level does autonomic dysreflexia occur?
backHtml: At or above about T6 (above the splanchnic sympathetic outflow).

frontHtml: Why does a posterior communicating artery aneurysm dilate the pupil?
backHtml: Pupillary parasympathetic fibres lie on the surface of the oculomotor nerve and are compressed first.

frontHtml: Head tilt and diplopia pattern of a right trochlear nerve palsy?
backHtml: Vertical diplopia worse looking down and in; head tilted to the left (away from the lesion).

frontHtml: Which cranial nerve runs free in the cavernous sinus beside the carotid artery?
backHtml: The abducens nerve (VI).

frontHtml: Which trigeminal division does not pass through the cavernous sinus?
backHtml: V3 (mandibular): it leaves through the foramen ovale.

frontHtml: Vagus lesion: which way does the uvula deviate?
backHtml: Away from the side of the lesion.

frontHtml: Hypoglossal lesion: which way does the tongue deviate?
backHtml: Toward the side of the lesion.

frontHtml: Which nerves pass through the jugular foramen?
backHtml: Glossopharyngeal (IX), vagus (X) and accessory (XI).

frontHtml: Why can a thoracic aortic aneurysm cause hoarseness?
backHtml: The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch.

frontHtml: Jaw deviation with a lower motor neuron V3 lesion?
backHtml: Toward the weak side (the opposite lateral pterygoid pushes it across).

frontHtml: Erb palsy: roots and arm position?
backHtml: C5–C6 (upper trunk): arm adducted, internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated.

frontHtml: Klumpke palsy plus ptosis and miosis: why the eye signs?
backHtml: The T1 root carries preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head (Horner syndrome).

frontHtml: Midshaft humerus fracture: nerve, deficit, and is triceps spared?
backHtml: Radial nerve in the spiral groove: wrist and finger drop; triceps usually spared.

frontHtml: Why is central palm sensation spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
backHtml: The palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve passes above the flexor retinaculum.

frontHtml: Ulnar lesion at Guyon canal vs elbow: which sensory area separates them?
backHtml: The dorsal medial hand: spared at the wrist (dorsal cutaneous branch leaves proximally), lost at the elbow.

frontHtml: Anterior interosseous nerve palsy: what can't the patient do, and is sensation lost?
backHtml: Cannot flex the tips of the thumb and index finger (circle collapses); no sensory loss.

frontHtml: Foot drop with weak inversion: root or fibular nerve?
backHtml: L5 root; inversion (tibialis posterior) is tibial nerve, spared in fibular neuropathy.

frontHtml: Anticoagulated patient, groin pain, weak knee extension, lost knee jerk: nerve and cause?
backHtml: Femoral nerve compressed by an iliopsoas haematoma.

frontHtml: Trendelenburg sign: which nerve and which side drops?
backHtml: Superior gluteal nerve; the pelvis drops on the side opposite the stance leg.

frontHtml: Mononeuritis multiplex most often signals what?
backHtml: Vasculitis of the vasa nervorum (e.g. polyarteritis nodosa, ANCA vasculitis, cryoglobulinaemia).

frontHtml: Gene and inheritance of Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A?
backHtml: PMP22 duplication, autosomal dominant; demyelinating.

frontHtml: Which fibres carry slow, burning second pain?
backHtml: Unmyelinated C fibres (A-delta fibres carry fast, sharp first pain).

frontHtml: Gabapentin and pregabalin bind what?
backHtml: The α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels.

frontHtml: Why do SNRIs and tricyclics relieve neuropathic pain?
backHtml: They strengthen descending serotonergic and noradrenergic inhibition of the dorsal horn.

frontHtml: HLA allele to test before carbamazepine in at-risk Asian ancestry?
backHtml: HLA-B*15:02 (SJS/TEN risk).

frontHtml: Dejerine–Roussy syndrome: lesion and symptom?
backHtml: VPL/VPM thalamus stroke; delayed burning pain and allodynia in the numb half of the body.

frontHtml: Capsaicin acts on which receptor?
backHtml: TRPV1; high doses defunctionalise nociceptor terminals.

frontHtml: First imaging for suspected spinal epidural abscess or cord compression?
backHtml: MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium (CT myelography if MRI contraindicated).

frontHtml: Cancer patient with back pain and new leg weakness: first treatment?
backHtml: High-dose dexamethasone at once, then emergency MRI and radiotherapy or surgery.

frontHtml: Most common organism in spinal epidural abscess?
backHtml: Staphylococcus aureus (cover MRSA empirically).

frontHtml: Which procedure is avoided in suspected epidural abscess?
backHtml: Lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: Vasopressor of choice in neurogenic shock with bradycardia?
backHtml: Norepinephrine (pure α-agonists can worsen bradycardia).

frontHtml: First steps in autonomic dysreflexia?
backHtml: Sit the patient up, loosen clothing, check the bladder and catheter, then bowel; antihypertensive only if pressure stays high.

frontHtml: Is high-dose methylprednisolone routine after acute spinal cord injury?
backHtml: No: doubtful benefit, real harms.

frontHtml: Longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis: which antibody to test?
backHtml: Aquaporin-4 IgG (and MOG IgG).

frontHtml: Older adult with clumsy hands, gait imbalance and Hoffmann sign: test?
backHtml: MRI of the cervical spine (degenerative cervical myelopathy).

frontHtml: When should acute sciatica without red flags be imaged?
backHtml: After about 6 weeks of persistent symptoms in a candidate for intervention, or sooner with red flags or a progressive deficit.

frontHtml: Initial treatment of acute sciatica without red flags?
backHtml: Stay active, heat, an NSAID; avoid bed rest and routine opioids.

frontHtml: Lost Achilles reflex points to which root?
backHtml: S1.

frontHtml: Double vision that persists with the other eye covered: where is the problem?
backHtml: In the eye itself (monocular diplopia): refractive error, cataract, cornea.

frontHtml: Painful third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil: next step?
backHtml: Emergency CT or MR angiography for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

frontHtml: Pituitary apoplexy with hypotension: first treatment?
backHtml: IV hydrocortisone, then MRI and neurosurgery.

frontHtml: Unexplained left vocal fold paralysis in a smoker: next test?
backHtml: CT from skull base to chest along the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

frontHtml: Shoulder droop and weak shrug after posterior triangle node biopsy: nerve?
backHtml: Spinal accessory nerve.

frontHtml: First-line treatment of mild carpal tunnel syndrome?
backHtml: Neutral night wrist splint (± steroid injection); surgery for wasting, weakness or severe conduction findings.

frontHtml: Bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome can be an early sign of which systemic disease?
backHtml: Transthyretin amyloidosis (also hypothyroidism, acromegaly, RA, diabetes, pregnancy).

frontHtml: Meralgia paresthetica: nerve and treatment?
backHtml: Lateral femoral cutaneous nerve; remove compression (belts, tight clothing), weight loss, reassurance.

frontHtml: Newborn Erb palsy: initial management and when to refer?
backHtml: Gentle range-of-motion exercises; refer if biceps function has not recovered by about 3–6 months.

frontHtml: Highest-yield blood tests for distal symmetric polyneuropathy?
backHtml: Glucose tolerance/HbA1c, B12 (± MMA), serum immunofixation.

frontHtml: When to start neuropathy screening in type 2 and type 1 diabetes?
backHtml: Type 2: at diagnosis; type 1: 5 years after diagnosis; then yearly.

frontHtml: Components of the annual diabetic foot sensory screen?
backHtml: 10-g monofilament plus one other test (pinprick, temperature or 128-Hz vibration).

frontHtml: ANCA-negative mononeuritis multiplex with hepatitis B and hypertension: diagnosis?
backHtml: Polyarteritis nodosa.

frontHtml: First-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia?
backHtml: Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine).

frontHtml: Trigeminal neuralgia features that suggest MS or a tumour?
backHtml: Young age, sensory loss, bilateral pain; image every patient with MRI.

frontHtml: Durable treatment for drug-refractory trigeminal neuralgia in a fit patient?
backHtml: Microvascular decompression.

frontHtml: Who should receive the recombinant zoster vaccine?
backHtml: Adults ≥50, and immunocompromised adults ≥19; 2 doses 2–6 months apart.

frontHtml: Cornerstone of CRPS treatment?
backHtml: Early graded physical and occupational therapy; avoid immobilisation.

frontHtml: Painful diabetic neuropathy with depression: preferred drug?
backHtml: Duloxetine (avoid with severe kidney impairment).

frontHtml: Alzheimer disease: what is outside the neuron and what is inside?
backHtml: Outside: amyloid-beta plaques (from APP cut by beta- then gamma-secretase). Inside: neurofibrillary tangles of hyperphosphorylated tau.

frontHtml: Which loss of cholinergic neurons underlies the use of cholinesterase inhibitors in Alzheimer disease?
backHtml: Loss of the nucleus basalis of Meynert, which supplies acetylcholine to the cortex.

frontHtml: Name three genes for autosomal dominant early-onset Alzheimer disease and their chromosomes.
backHtml: APP (21), PSEN1 (14), PSEN2 (1).

frontHtml: Main adverse effect of lecanemab and donanemab, and who is at highest risk?
backHtml: ARIA: vasogenic edema and microhemorrhage/siderosis; highest in APOE e4 homozygotes.

frontHtml: Personality change, disinhibition and sweet cravings at 58 with good memory: diagnosis and pathology?
backHtml: Frontotemporal dementia: frontal and anterior temporal atrophy with tau (Pick bodies) or TDP-43 inclusions.

frontHtml: Four core features of dementia with Lewy bodies?
backHtml: Fluctuating cognition, recurrent visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, parkinsonism.

frontHtml: Which four enzymes need thiamine pyrophosphate?
backHtml: Pyruvate dehydrogenase, alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase, branched-chain ketoacid dehydrogenase and transketolase.

frontHtml: Classic findings of Wernicke encephalopathy?
backHtml: Confusion, eye movement abnormalities (nystagmus, lateral rectus palsy) and gait ataxia; often incomplete.

frontHtml: Korsakoff syndrome: memory pattern and key lesion?
backHtml: Anterograde (and some retrograde) amnesia with confabulation; mammillary bodies and medial dorsal thalamus.

frontHtml: Hours of anterograde amnesia with repetitive questioning and preserved identity after cold water swimming?
backHtml: Transient global amnesia; benign, resolves within 24 hours.

frontHtml: ALS: which motor neurons, and what is spared?
backHtml: Upper and lower motor neurons; sensation, eye movements and sphincters are spared.

frontHtml: Mechanism of nusinersen versus onasemnogene abeparvovec in SMA?
backHtml: Nusinersen: antisense oligonucleotide that makes SMN2 keep exon 7. Onasemnogene: AAV9 vector carrying a working SMN1.

frontHtml: Myasthenia gravis versus Lambert-Eaton syndrome: effect of repeated effort?
backHtml: MG: weakness worsens. LEMS: strength and reflexes briefly improve.

frontHtml: Lambert-Eaton syndrome: antibody target and associated tumour?
backHtml: Presynaptic P/Q-type voltage-gated calcium channels; small cell lung cancer.

frontHtml: How does botulinum toxin cause paralysis?
backHtml: Its protease cleaves SNARE proteins, so acetylcholine vesicles cannot fuse and release.

frontHtml: Name drug classes that can worsen myasthenia gravis.
backHtml: Aminoglycosides, fluoroquinolones, macrolides, magnesium, beta-blockers, immune checkpoint inhibitors.

frontHtml: Duchenne versus Becker: what does the dystrophin mutation do to the reading frame?
backHtml: Duchenne: frameshift, almost no dystrophin. Becker: in-frame, shorter partly working dystrophin.

frontHtml: Why are the calves big in Duchenne muscular dystrophy?
backHtml: Pseudohypertrophy: muscle replaced by fat and fibrous tissue.

frontHtml: Myotonic dystrophy type 1: mutation and four non-muscle features?
backHtml: CTG repeat in DMPK; cataracts, frontal balding, cardiac conduction block, insulin resistance (also testicular atrophy).

frontHtml: Which organism and mechanism link diarrhea to Guillain-Barré syndrome?
backHtml: Campylobacter jejuni; antibodies to its lipooligosaccharide cross-react with nerve gangliosides (molecular mimicry).

frontHtml: Miller Fisher syndrome: triad and antibody?
backHtml: Ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; anti-GQ1b.

frontHtml: Dopamine acts on which receptor in each basal ganglia pathway, and with what effect?
backHtml: Direct pathway: D1, excites. Indirect pathway: D2, inhibits. Both favour movement.

frontHtml: A lesion of which nucleus causes contralateral hemiballismus?
backHtml: The subthalamic nucleus.

frontHtml: Which striatal neurons die first in Huntington disease?
backHtml: Indirect-pathway (D2) neurons projecting to the external globus pallidus, causing chorea.

frontHtml: Why is carbidopa given with levodopa?
backHtml: It blocks peripheral DOPA decarboxylase and does not enter the brain, so less nausea and more levodopa reaches the CNS.

frontHtml: Dopamine agonist adverse effect to ask about at every visit?
backHtml: Impulse control disorders: gambling, shopping, binge eating, hypersexuality.

frontHtml: Wilson disease: gene, protein function and eye sign?
backHtml: ATP7B, hepatocyte copper ATPase that loads ceruloplasmin and excretes copper into bile; Kayser-Fleischer rings.

frontHtml: How does ammonia injure the brain in hepatic encephalopathy?
backHtml: Astrocytes make glutamine from ammonia; glutamine accumulates and the astrocytes swell.

frontHtml: Osmotic demyelination syndrome: cause and timing?
backHtml: Correcting chronic hyponatremia too quickly; dysarthria, dysphagia and quadriparesis appear days later.

frontHtml: B12 versus folate deficiency: methylmalonic acid and homocysteine?
backHtml: B12: both high. Folate: homocysteine high, methylmalonic acid normal.

frontHtml: Cherry-red spot: how do you tell Tay-Sachs from Niemann-Pick type A?
backHtml: Tay-Sachs has no hepatosplenomegaly (hexosaminidase A); Niemann-Pick has it (sphingomyelinase).

frontHtml: X-linked adrenoleukodystrophy: defect and what accumulates?
backHtml: ABCD1 peroxisomal transporter; very-long-chain fatty acids, in adrenal cortex and white matter.

frontHtml: Muscle biopsy hallmark of mitochondrial encephalomyopathies?
backHtml: Ragged red fibres on modified Gomori trichrome.

frontHtml: Which blood tests are part of the basic dementia work-up?
backHtml: Blood count, metabolic panel with calcium and glucose, vitamin B12 and TSH; syphilis and HIV if at risk.

frontHtml: Normal pressure hydrocephalus: order of symptoms and the test that predicts shunt response?
backHtml: Gait, then urinary urgency, then cognitive slowing; large-volume lumbar tap with gait testing.

frontHtml: What must be done before starting an anti-amyloid antibody?
backHtml: Confirm amyloid (PET or CSF), a recent brain MRI, APOE counseling, review of anticoagulants; MRI monitoring for ARIA.

frontHtml: First step for new evening agitation in a nursing home resident with dementia?
backHtml: Look for pain, constipation, retention, infection and environmental triggers; non-drug measures first.

frontHtml: Why avoid antipsychotics in dementia when possible?
backHtml: They raise mortality and stroke risk in older adults with dementia.

frontHtml: Bedside thresholds for elective intubation in neuromuscular weakness?
backHtml: FVC below about 20 mL/kg, NIF weaker than about −30 cm H2O, a rapid fall, or pooling secretions.

frontHtml: Guillain-Barré syndrome treatment and what does not work?
backHtml: IVIG or plasma exchange (equal); corticosteroids do not help.

frontHtml: After diagnosing myasthenia gravis, which imaging is needed?
backHtml: Chest CT or MRI for thymoma.

frontHtml: Treatment of infant botulism?
backHtml: Human botulism immune globulin early, supportive care; avoid aminoglycosides.

frontHtml: When should noninvasive ventilation start in ALS?
backHtml: When FVC falls below about 50% predicted or orthopnea or nocturnal hypoventilation symptoms appear.

frontHtml: First-line drug for Parkinson disease that limits function in a 76-year-old?
backHtml: Carbidopa-levodopa.

frontHtml: Order of drug withdrawal for psychosis in Parkinson disease?
backHtml: Anticholinergics, amantadine, MAO-B inhibitors, dopamine agonists, COMT inhibitors; reduce levodopa last.

frontHtml: Antipsychotics that can be used in Parkinson disease psychosis?
backHtml: Pimavanserin, low-dose quetiapine, clozapine; avoid haloperidol and risperidone.

frontHtml: Essential tremor first-line drugs?
backHtml: Propranolol or primidone (primidone if asthma).

frontHtml: Tardive dyskinesia treatment?
backHtml: A VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine, deutetrabenazine); review the antipsychotic; anticholinergics worsen it.

frontHtml: Acute dystonic reaction treatment?
backHtml: IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine.

frontHtml: Is a blood ammonia level needed to diagnose or follow hepatic encephalopathy?
backHtml: No; diagnosis is clinical, and levels do not guide treatment.

frontHtml: Hepatic encephalopathy recurrence despite lactulose: next drug?
backHtml: Rifaximin.

frontHtml: Severe symptomatic hyponatremia: first treatment?
backHtml: 100 mL of 3% saline, repeated up to twice, for a 4–6 mEq/L rise.

frontHtml: Maximum 24-hour sodium rise in a patient at high risk of osmotic demyelination?
backHtml: About 8 mEq/L.

frontHtml: How do you reverse overcorrection of hyponatremia?
backHtml: Stop saline; give 5% dextrose in water and desmopressin.

frontHtml: A B12-like myelopathy with cytopenias, normal B12 and heavy denture cream use?
backHtml: Copper deficiency from zinc excess; check serum copper and ceruloplasmin.

frontHtml: Which antiseizure drug blocks thalamic T-type calcium channels, and for which seizure type?
backHtml: Ethosuximide: absence seizures only.

frontHtml: Benzodiazepines versus barbiturates at the GABA<sub>A</sub> receptor?
backHtml: Benzodiazepines increase the frequency of channel opening; barbiturates increase its duration (and can open it directly at high doses).

frontHtml: Which antiseizure drug binds synaptic vesicle protein SV2A?
backHtml: Levetiracetam (and brivaracetam).

frontHtml: Commonest pathology behind drug-resistant temporal lobe epilepsy in adults?
backHtml: Hippocampal sclerosis: neuron loss and gliosis, worst in CA1.

frontHtml: Which antiseizure drugs can worsen absence and myoclonic seizures?
backHtml: Sodium channel blockers such as carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine and phenytoin.

frontHtml: What causes the visual aura of migraine?
backHtml: Cortical spreading depolarization: a slow wave of depolarization, then suppression, crossing the occipital cortex.

frontHtml: Triptan receptor targets and the main contraindication?
backHtml: 5-HT1B/1D agonists; avoid in coronary, cerebrovascular or peripheral arterial disease.

frontHtml: Which migraine antibody binds the CGRP receptor rather than CGRP itself?
backHtml: Erenumab.

frontHtml: Pathway for tearing in cluster headache?
backHtml: Superior salivatory nucleus → facial nerve (greater petrosal) → pterygopalatine ganglion → lacrimal gland.

frontHtml: EEG hallmark of N2 sleep?
backHtml: Sleep spindles and K complexes.

frontHtml: Which sleep stage dominates the first third of the night, and which parasomnias arise from it?
backHtml: N3 (slow-wave); sleepwalking and sleep terrors.

frontHtml: Cause of narcolepsy type 1?
backHtml: Loss of orexin (hypocretin) neurons in the lateral hypothalamus; linked to HLA-DQB1*06:02.

frontHtml: REM sleep behavior disorder is an early sign of which group of diseases?
backHtml: α-Synucleinopathies: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy.

frontHtml: Mechanism of sodium oxybate?
backHtml: GABAB agonist (GHB); treats cataplexy and consolidates night sleep.

frontHtml: Sleep changes in major depression?
backHtml: Shorter REM latency, more REM, less N3, early morning waking.

frontHtml: Why does a small phenytoin dose increase cause toxicity?
backHtml: Its metabolism saturates: zero-order kinetics at usual doses.

frontHtml: Genetic marker to test before carbamazepine in patients of Asian ancestry?
backHtml: HLA-B*15:02 (risk of SJS/TEN).

frontHtml: Why do isoniazid-induced seizures resist benzodiazepines?
backHtml: Pyridoxal phosphate depletion cuts GABA synthesis (glutamate decarboxylase); give IV pyridoxine.

frontHtml: Topiramate: mechanism behind its kidney stones?
backHtml: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition causes acidosis and alkaline urine, which favour calcium phosphate stones.

frontHtml: Rigidity with slow reflexes versus clonus with brisk reflexes?
backHtml: Rigidity: neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Clonus: serotonin syndrome.

frontHtml: Standard evaluation after a first unprovoked seizure with normal labs?
backHtml: Brain MRI and EEG.

frontHtml: Antiseizure drugs for a person with generalized epilepsy who could become pregnant?
backHtml: Levetiracetam or lamotrigine (avoid valproate), plus folic acid before conception.

frontHtml: Definition of a simple febrile seizure?
backHtml: Generalized, under 15 minutes, once in 24 hours, in a feverish child aged 6 months to 5 years.

frontHtml: Diagnostic standard for functional (psychogenic nonepileptic) seizures?
backHtml: Video-EEG capturing a typical event without epileptic EEG change.

frontHtml: First drug for convulsive status epilepticus without IV access?
backHtml: IM midazolam.

frontHtml: Second-line drugs when status epilepticus continues after benzodiazepines?
backHtml: IV levetiracetam, fosphenytoin or valproate.

frontHtml: Patient does not wake after convulsions stop. What next?
backHtml: EEG for nonconvulsive status epilepticus.

frontHtml: Acute treatment of a cluster headache attack?
backHtml: 100% oxygen at 12–15 L/min by non-rebreather, or subcutaneous sumatriptan.

frontHtml: Which contraceptives are contraindicated in migraine with aura?
backHtml: Estrogen-containing methods (pill, patch, ring).

frontHtml: Thresholds for medication-overuse headache?
backHtml: Simple analgesics on 15 or more days a month; triptans, opioids or combination analgesics on 10 or more.

frontHtml: Thunderclap headache with a negative CT more than 6 hours after onset: next step?
backHtml: Lumbar puncture (or CT angiography).

frontHtml: First-line treatment for chronic insomnia?
backHtml: CBT-I.

frontHtml: MSLT criteria supporting narcolepsy?
backHtml: Mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less with 2 or more sleep-onset REM periods.

frontHtml: Iron threshold for treating restless legs syndrome?
backHtml: Ferritin 75 ng/mL or less or transferrin saturation under 20%.

frontHtml: Preferred first-line drugs for restless legs syndrome, and why not dopamine agonists?
backHtml: α2δ ligands (gabapentin enacarbil, gabapentin, pregabalin); dopamine agonists cause augmentation.

frontHtml: Why avoid adaptive servo-ventilation in central sleep apnea with HFrEF?
backHtml: It increased mortality when the ejection fraction is 45% or less.

frontHtml: Light therapy for delayed versus advanced sleep phase?
backHtml: Delayed: morning light. Advanced: evening light.

frontHtml: Treatment of acute dystonia from metoclopramide?
backHtml: IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine.

frontHtml: Treatment of tardive dyskinesia when the antipsychotic must continue?
backHtml: Add a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine).

frontHtml: Why avoid flumazenil in an unknown overdose?
backHtml: It can provoke seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent patients or after tricyclic co-ingestion.

frontHtml: Drug for painful chemotherapy-induced neuropathy?
backHtml: Duloxetine.

frontHtml: Confusion with high ammonia and normal liver tests on valproate?
backHtml: Valproate hyperammonemic encephalopathy: stop valproate, give levocarnitine.

frontHtml: Management of PRES on tacrolimus?
backHtml: Lower the blood pressure and reduce or switch the calcineurin inhibitor.

frontHtml: Neonatal conjunctivitis: typical day of onset for chemical, gonococcal and chlamydial causes?
backHtml: Chemical: first day. Gonococcal: about days 2–5. Chlamydial: about days 5–14.

frontHtml: Which organism classically causes keratitis in a contact lens wearer who sleeps in the lenses?
backHtml: Pseudomonas aeruginosa, which can melt the cornea within a day.

frontHtml: Branching corneal ulcer with terminal bulbs on fluorescein staining: cause, and where does the virus hide?
backHtml: Herpes simplex keratitis; latent in the trigeminal ganglion.

frontHtml: Episcleritis versus scleritis: what does phenylephrine do to the red vessels?
backHtml: Episcleral vessels blanch; the deep vessels in scleritis do not.

frontHtml: Through which structure does ethmoid sinusitis spread into the orbit?
backHtml: The thin medial orbital wall, the lamina papyracea.

frontHtml: Why can orbital infection cause cavernous sinus thrombosis?
backHtml: The ophthalmic veins have no valves and drain into the cavernous sinus.

frontHtml: What does the RB protein do when it is unphosphorylated?
backHtml: It binds and inactivates E2F, blocking the G1-to-S transition until cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates it.

frontHtml: Bilateral retinoblastoma implies what about the RB1 mutation?
backHtml: It is germline (heritable): only one more somatic hit is needed in any retinal cell.

frontHtml: Characteristic second cancer in survivors of heritable retinoblastoma?
backHtml: Osteosarcoma (also soft-tissue sarcomas and melanoma).

frontHtml: Most common intraocular malignancy in adults overall, and most common primary one?
backHtml: Overall: metastasis to the choroid (breast, lung). Primary: uveal melanoma.

frontHtml: Where does uveal melanoma metastasise, and why not to lymph nodes?
backHtml: To the liver, through the blood; the inside of the globe has no lymphatics.

frontHtml: Most common eyelid malignancy and its histology?
backHtml: Basal cell carcinoma: basaloid nests with peripheral palisading; usually lower lid.

frontHtml: Two routes of aqueous outflow?
backHtml: Trabecular meshwork to Schlemm's canal (main), and the uveoscleral route through the ciliary muscle.

frontHtml: Latanoprost: mechanism and two cosmetic adverse effects?
backHtml: Increases uveoscleral outflow; darkens the iris and lengthens lashes.

frontHtml: Which glaucoma drug classes reduce aqueous production?
backHtml: β-Blockers, α2-agonists and carbonic anhydrase inhibitors.

frontHtml: Lens dislocation direction: Marfan versus homocystinuria?
backHtml: Marfan: usually up and out. Homocystinuria: usually down and in.

frontHtml: Which cataract is typical of long-term corticosteroid use?
backHtml: Posterior subcapsular cataract (glare, poor near vision).

frontHtml: Myopia: where is the focus, and which lens corrects it?
backHtml: In front of the retina; a diverging (concave, minus) lens.

frontHtml: Cause of presbyopia?
backHtml: Age-related loss of lens elasticity, so the lens cannot round up for near focus.

frontHtml: Bitemporal hemianopia: where is the lesion and the usual cause?
backHtml: Optic chiasm; usually a pituitary adenoma pressing from below.

frontHtml: Contralateral upper quadrantanopia localises to?
backHtml: Meyer loop in the temporal lobe.

frontHtml: Homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing localises to?
backHtml: The occipital cortex, usually a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

frontHtml: Swinging-flashlight test: both pupils dilate when the light moves to the left eye. Meaning?
backHtml: A left relative afferent pupillary defect (left optic nerve disease).

frontHtml: Classic triad of Horner syndrome?
backHtml: Mild ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis (anhidrosis spared in most third-order lesions).

frontHtml: Pupils that constrict to near effort but not to light, in tertiary syphilis?
backHtml: Argyll Robertson pupils (dorsal midbrain, near the pretectal area).

frontHtml: Why does a compressive oculomotor palsy dilate the pupil?
backHtml: Parasympathetic pupillary fibres run on the outside of the nerve and are compressed first.

frontHtml: Which cranial nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia worse when reading, with a head tilt away from the affected side?
backHtml: Trochlear (IV) nerve palsy (superior oblique).

frontHtml: On right gaze the left eye fails to adduct and the right eye has nystagmus; convergence is normal. Lesion?
backHtml: Left MLF: left internuclear ophthalmoplegia.

frontHtml: Why is the abducens nerve a false-localising sign in raised intracranial pressure?
backHtml: Its long course along the clivus makes it easy to stretch.

frontHtml: Strongest modifiable risk factor for thyroid eye disease?
backHtml: Smoking.

frontHtml: Define amblyopia and its main causes.
backHtml: Cortical suppression of an eye's image in early childhood, from strabismus, anisometropia or a blocked visual axis.

frontHtml: Red-eye red flags that need same-day ophthalmology?
backHtml: Moderate or severe pain, photophobia, reduced acuity, corneal opacity, abnormal pupil, contact lens wear, recent surgery or trauma, newborn.

frontHtml: Treatment of neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis?
backHtml: A single parenteral dose of ceftriaxone, eye irrigation, admission and evaluation for disseminated infection.

frontHtml: Why does neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis need systemic, not topical, treatment?
backHtml: To clear nasopharyngeal carriage and prevent afebrile pneumonia.

frontHtml: Two things never to do for a suspected contact lens corneal ulcer?
backHtml: Never patch it and never start steroid drops.

frontHtml: Emergency treatment of endophthalmitis after cataract surgery?
backHtml: Vitreous tap and intravitreal antibiotics (for example vancomycin plus ceftazidime); vitrectomy if vision is very poor.

frontHtml: Findings that separate orbital from preseptal cellulitis?
backHtml: Pain with eye movement, restricted movement, proptosis, reduced vision or an afferent pupillary defect.

frontHtml: Next step for an infant with an absent or white red reflex?
backHtml: Urgent ophthalmology referral for a dilated examination.

frontHtml: Preferred imaging to stage retinoblastoma, and why not CT?
backHtml: MRI of brain and orbits; CT radiation raises second-cancer risk in germline carriers.

frontHtml: What should siblings of a child with heritable retinoblastoma receive?
backHtml: Testing for the family's RB1 mutation and serial dilated fundus examinations from birth.

frontHtml: Staging and surveillance focus for uveal melanoma?
backHtml: Liver imaging and liver function tests.

frontHtml: A chalazion recurs in the same place in a 72-year-old. Next step?
backHtml: Full-thickness biopsy to exclude sebaceous gland carcinoma.

frontHtml: Immediate drugs for acute angle-closure glaucoma?
backHtml: Topical β-blocker and α2-agonist, systemic acetazolamide, then pilocarpine as pressure falls; mannitol if needed.

frontHtml: Definitive treatment after an angle-closure attack, and what about the other eye?
backHtml: Laser peripheral iridotomy, plus a prophylactic iridotomy in the fellow eye.

frontHtml: First-line treatments for primary open-angle glaucoma?
backHtml: A prostaglandin analogue drop or selective laser trabeculoplasty.

frontHtml: Bilateral angle closure with a sudden myopic shift soon after starting a migraine drug?
backHtml: Topiramate: stop it; use aqueous suppressants and cycloplegia, not iridotomy.

frontHtml: When is cataract surgery offered?
backHtml: When the cataract limits daily activities such as driving or reading.

frontHtml: Dry eyes with a dry mouth and dental caries: which antibodies?
backHtml: Anti-Ro/SSA and anti-La/SSB (Sjögren syndrome).

frontHtml: Anisocoria greater in the dark versus greater in bright light: which pupil is abnormal?
backHtml: Dark: the small pupil fails to dilate (Horner). Light: the large pupil fails to constrict (CN III, tonic pupil, drug).

frontHtml: Painful oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil: next step?
backHtml: Emergency CT or MR angiography for a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

frontHtml: Acute painful Horner syndrome after neck manipulation: diagnosis and test?
backHtml: Carotid dissection; CT or MR angiography of head and neck.

frontHtml: Eye-drop test that confirms Horner syndrome?
backHtml: Apraclonidine dilates the Horner pupil and reverses the anisocoria.

frontHtml: First-line treatment for active moderate-to-severe thyroid eye disease?
backHtml: IV methylprednisolone pulses (teprotumumab is an alternative); stop smoking.

frontHtml: Treatment of amblyopia after correcting the refraction?
backHtml: Patch the stronger eye (or atropine in the stronger eye).

frontHtml: Which circulation supplies the photoreceptors and the fovea?
backHtml: The choroid (ciliary arteries). The central retinal artery supplies the inner two-thirds of the retina.

frontHtml: Why is the fovea red in central retinal artery occlusion?
backHtml: The fovea has no inner retinal layers to whiten, so the normal choroid shows through, surrounded by pale ischaemic retina.

frontHtml: Earliest histological and earliest clinical sign of diabetic retinopathy?
backHtml: Histological: loss of pericytes. Clinical: microaneurysms.

frontHtml: What drives new vessel growth in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, wet AMD and retinopathy of prematurity?
backHtml: VEGF released by ischaemic or hypoxic retina.

frontHtml: Fundus with haemorrhages in all four quadrants and dilated tortuous veins?
backHtml: Central retinal vein occlusion (risk: hypertension, age, diabetes, glaucoma).

frontHtml: Night blindness, then tunnel vision, with bone-spicule pigment: which cells fail first?
backHtml: Rods (retinitis pigmentosa, a rod-cone dystrophy).

frontHtml: Why does papilloedema swell the disc?
backHtml: Raised intracranial pressure in the optic nerve sheath stops axoplasmic flow, so axons swell at the disc.

frontHtml: Why are alkali eye burns usually worse than acid burns?
backHtml: Alkali saponifies lipids and causes liquefactive necrosis that keeps penetrating; acid causes coagulative necrosis that forms a barrier.

frontHtml: Orbital floor fracture: which muscle is trapped and which nerve is injured?
backHtml: Inferior rectus (limited upgaze) and the infraorbital nerve (V2; numb cheek and upper lip).

frontHtml: Afferent and efferent limbs of the oculocardiac reflex?
backHtml: Afferent: trigeminal (V1). Efferent: vagus (bradycardia, nausea).

frontHtml: Signs of an open globe?
backHtml: Peaked or teardrop pupil, shallow chamber, extensive subconjunctival haemorrhage, low pressure, positive Seidel sign.

frontHtml: Why is a hyphema more dangerous in sickle cell disease or trait?
backHtml: Red cells sickle in the low-oxygen aqueous and block the trabecular meshwork, so pressure rises more.

frontHtml: Which cataract do glucocorticoids cause?
backHtml: Posterior subcapsular cataract. Steroids can also raise intraocular pressure.

frontHtml: How does topiramate cause angle closure?
backHtml: Ciliochoroidal effusion rotates the lens-iris diaphragm forward: bilateral closure with myopic shift, no pupillary block.

frontHtml: Tamsulosin and cataract surgery?
backHtml: Alpha-1A blockade weakens the iris dilator: intraoperative floppy iris syndrome.

frontHtml: Which drug tints vision blue, and which tints it yellow?
backHtml: Blue: PDE5 inhibitors (via retinal PDE6). Yellow: digoxin toxicity.

frontHtml: Ethambutol eye toxicity?
backHtml: Optic neuropathy: falling acuity, red-green colour loss, central scotoma; worse with renal impairment.

frontHtml: Why can timolol eye drops cause bronchospasm?
backHtml: Non-selective beta-blocker absorbed through the nasal mucosa, bypassing first-pass metabolism.

frontHtml: First step for acute central retinal artery occlusion?
backHtml: Treat as a stroke: immediate transfer to a stroke centre; check ESR/CRP if over 50.

frontHtml: Giant cell arteritis with visual loss: first step?
backHtml: High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone now; biopsy afterward.

frontHtml: When does retinopathy screening start in type 1 and type 2 diabetes?
backHtml: Type 2: at diagnosis. Type 1: within 5 years of onset. Then yearly (1–2 yearly if normal and well controlled).

frontHtml: First-line treatment for centre-involving diabetic macular oedema with reduced vision?
backHtml: Intravitreal anti-VEGF injections.

frontHtml: Intermediate dry AMD in a smoker: what supplement?
backHtml: AREDS2-type: vitamins C and E, zinc, copper, lutein, zeaxanthin; no beta-carotene.

frontHtml: Bilateral disc swelling: first test?
backHtml: MRI of the brain with MR venography, before lumbar puncture.

frontHtml: Retinopathy of prematurity screening criteria (US)?
backHtml: Born at 30 weeks or less or weighing 1,500 g or less, plus selected larger unstable infants.

frontHtml: Chemical splash to the eye: first step?
backHtml: Irrigate immediately, before acuity, until the tear pH is neutral (about 7.0–7.5).

frontHtml: Corneal abrasion in a contact lens wearer: treatment?
backHtml: Anti-pseudomonal fluoroquinolone drops, no lens wear, no patch, no take-home anaesthetic.

frontHtml: Open globe: what to do and what to avoid?
backHtml: Rigid shield, antiemetic, analgesia, systemic antibiotics, tetanus, CT. Avoid pressure, tonometry and drops.

frontHtml: Post-traumatic proptosis, tense orbit, falling vision and RAPD: next step?
backHtml: Bedside lateral canthotomy and inferior cantholysis, before imaging.

frontHtml: Suspected metallic intraocular foreign body: imaging?
backHtml: CT of the orbits; MRI is contraindicated.

frontHtml: Child with orbital floor fracture, quiet eye, bradycardia and vomiting?
backHtml: Trapdoor fracture with entrapment and oculocardiac reflex: urgent surgical release.

frontHtml: Hydroxychloroquine screening plan?
backHtml: Dose at or below 5 mg/kg/day actual weight; baseline exam, then yearly from 5 years (sooner with risk factors); OCT plus visual fields.

frontHtml: Topiramate-induced angle closure: treatment?
backHtml: Stop topiramate; aqueous suppressants and cycloplegics. No pilocarpine, no iridotomy.

frontHtml: Patient on tamsulosin before cataract surgery?
backHtml: Tell the surgeon; stopping the drug does not reliably help.

frontHtml: Unexplained bradycardia in a glaucoma patient: which drop to suspect?
backHtml: Timolol; switch to a prostaglandin analogue.

frontHtml: Non-healing corneal defect in a patient using numbing drops at home?
backHtml: Topical anaesthetic toxic keratopathy: stop the drops, urgent ophthalmology.
